The treasure dates to the third or second century B.C.E., during the late Iron Age, but researchers don’t know much beyond that. The construction crew’s excavator destroyed the original context of the find, erasing potential clues as to how it ended up in the Danube in the first place. There’s no sign of a boat near where the iron bars were found. However, given the size and location of the cache, the researchers write in the paper that it’s “highly likely” the iron bars were being transported on the river and must have been lost in a shipwreck.

Whoever was supposed to receive the bars must have offered something very valuable in return, such as gold, silver, enslaved labor, cattle, horses, military service or a dowry, the researchers write.

Whatever the form of payment, the hoard demonstrates the “increased capacities of iron production that were reached in the [third and second century B.C.E.] in the Danube region,” Trebsche says in the statement.

Where the iron bars were forged isn’t clear, nor is where they were headed. However, the researchers suspect they were traveling downstream when they sank to the bottom of the river. That rules out iron-production districts farther east, including those in Burgenland. Instead, the bars were more likely made somewhere in Bavaria, where archaeologists have previously discovered iron-production sites near oppida—large, fortified European Iron Age towns.
By analyzing traces of elements in the bars, the researchers write, they hope to more accurately pinpoint where the raw metal used to make them originated.

Workers Extracting Gravel From the Danube River Dredged Up a 2,200-Year-Old ‘Rusty Treasure’ That Could Have Equipped an Army

The cache comprises the remains of at least 500 iron bars, which were likely headed downstream to be forged into finished products

Sarah Kuta
| Daily Correspondent

September 22, 2026 8:00 a.m.

Roughly 2,200 years ago, a vessel carrying at least 500 iron bars sank in the Danube River. The treasure remained hidden in the riverbed in what is now Upper Austria for centuries, until a construction crew accidentally unearthed it.

Now, archaeologists say the cache represents the largest single discovery of iron bars in Europe. They describe the “rusty treasure” in a paper published September 21 in the journal Antiquity.

The modern saga of the iron bars dates to 2019, when workers extracting gravel near the village of Deinham, on the right bank of the Danube, noticed that their excavator had pulled up several rusted, double-pointed iron objects. They figured the items might be significant, so they alerted Austria’s Federal Monuments Office.

Did you know? Austrian archaeology

Archaeologists excavating a rock salt mine in Austria recently discovered a well-preserved, 2,000-year-old child’s shoe.

“It is nothing short of a minor miracle that the largest mass find of prehistoric iron bars in Europe did not end up at scrap dealers,” lead author Peter Trebsche, an archaeologist at the University of Innsbruck, says in a statement.

After the initial report, archaeologists headed out to Deinham, where they painstakingly searched by hand through the crew’s gravel heaps to try to recover additional iron objects. They ended up with 193 complete iron bars and hundreds of fragments, which together amounted to at least 500 bars.

The bars are shaped “somewhat like a willow leaf,” Gayoung Lee writes for Gizmodo, with one pointed end and one flat. The complete bars are a little less than a foot long, on average, and weigh around 4.5 pounds. The entire cache would have weighed at least 2,200 pounds, the team estimates.

“A major challenge was the fact that most iron bars were still covered with gravel and sand, which we were not able to remove,” Trebsche tells Gizmodo. “Fortunately, about one-third of all bars had already been ‘cleaned’ by the gravel crusher in the gravel plant.”

Archaeologists suspect that the iron bars were not finished products. Instead, they believe they were roughly shaped, semi-processed objects that would have eventually been forged into other items. Based on their 2,200-pound calculation, the researchers say the iron would have been enough to make roughly 500 swords or up to 8,000 iron nails.

“Even if we take material losses during manufacture into account, the iron from Deinham would have been sufficient to equip a large group of warriors with weapons,” Trebsche says in the statement.

The treasure dates to the third or second century B.C.E., during the late Iron Age, but researchers don’t know much beyond that. The construction crew’s excavator destroyed the original context of the find, erasing potential clues as to how it ended up in the Danube in the first place. There’s no sign of a boat near where the iron bars were found. However, given the size and location of the cache, the researchers write in the paper that it’s “highly likely” the iron bars were being transported on the river and must have been lost in a shipwreck.

Transporting goods by boat was standard practice at the time. However, the researchers say that such a large quantity of iron for a single transaction is unusual. Whoever was supposed to receive the bars must have offered something very valuable in return, such as gold, silver, enslaved labor, cattle, horses, military service or a dowry, the researchers write.

Whatever the form of payment, the hoard demonstrates the “increased capacities of iron production that were reached in the [third and second century B.C.E.] in the Danube region,” Trebsche says in the statement.

Where the iron bars were forged isn’t clear, nor is where they were headed. However, the researchers suspect they were traveling downstream when they sank to the bottom of the river. That rules out iron-production districts farther east, including those in Burgenland. Instead, the bars were more likely made somewhere in Bavaria, where archaeologists have previously discovered iron-production sites near oppida—large, fortified European Iron Age towns.

By analyzing traces of elements in the bars, the researchers write, they hope to more accurately pinpoint where the raw metal used to make them originated.
